study.title: Esther 10 - The honour of Mordecai and the stability of the Jewish people
study.overview: The chapter ends with a brief picture of Persian power and the exaltation of Mordecai. First, King Ahasuerus imposes tribute on his vast dominion, showing the extent of his authority and the financial requirement of the empire. Then the text recalls that the king's deeds and the greatness of Mordecai were recorded in the royal annals of Media and Persia, underlining that God's history with his people also unfolds in the public and political field. Finally, Mordecai is presented as the second after the king, respected among the Jews and dedicated to the welfare of his people, speaking peace and prosperity for all.

outline.title: The King's tribute over the whole empire
outline.explanation: Ahasuerus imposes tribute on the land and on the islands of the sea. The verse highlights the extent of Persian power and also the administrative and economic weight of an imperial government over its domains.

outline.title: The Official Memory of the King and Mardokhou
outline.explanation: The text refers to the books of the chronicles of the kings of Middle and Persia, indicating that the feats of Ahasuerus and the elevation of Mordecai were not hidden events, but part of the public memory of the empire.

outline.title: Mordecai as a servant of the good of the people
outline.explanation: Mardoqueus is described as the Jew placed in a very high position, respected by his brothers and committed to the collective good. His way of acting contrasts with Haman's vanity and shows leadership focused on the prosperity of the people.

study.context: The notes point to the scenario of the Persian empire, with broad dominance and official government records. The chapter finalizes the book with a summary of the greatness of Ahasuerus and the honor of Mordecai. Mathew Henry's note notes that the continuation of the book beyond verse 3 appears only in Greek tradition, while the Hebrew text closes here; this is relevant to the final form of the chapter, but does not alter the central message of these verses.
study.theology: Theologically, the chapter shows that God can exalt his faithful servant within the political structure of a pagan empire. Mardoqueu is not presented as a conqueror of personal prestige, but as someone who seeks the good of his people and speaks in favor of the peace of all. There is here a vision of just and benevolent leadership, in contrast to selfishness and ostentation. The text also suggests that divine providence preserves the memory of the correct actions and places the just in a position of influence for the collective good.

scholarViews.insight: Mordecai did not magnify himself as Haman; he was a righteous man, who continually sought the good of others and was rewarded with a high position in government and with the high esteem of his people.
Mordecai is presented as a distinct blessing for his people, for the chapter describes him as a great one among the Jews and at the same time connected to their good.
Mardoqueus was the second after the king, that is, the prime minister, and dedicated himself to promoting the interest of his people and establishing his prosperity.

questions: What does the contrast between Haman and Mordecai teach about ambition and service to others?
In what ways can the position of authority be used to speak peace and prosperity to the people?
How can the memory of the acts of God and his servants strengthen the faithfulness of the community?
study.practice: This text invites the reader to measure success not by personal promotion, but by service to the common good. In practice, this means using influence, resources and words to promote peace, justice and real prosperity around, especially among the brothers in faith and in the community in general. It also encourages to accept that God sees and preserves what is done with righteousness, even when honor comes through public and political paths.
study.uncertainty: The chapter is short and the received text closes in verse 3. The notes mention that ancient traditions, such as Greek and Latin, continue the book beyond that point, but this does not belong to the biblical passage provided here. In addition, the exact identification of the king with specific historical figures appears in the notes as a hypothesis, not as a certainty of the text itself.
